match.reason: The bank point teaches general Year 7 discussion etiquette such as listening, building on ideas and disagreeing politely, but the new point needs a Year 10 skill of stating an evidence-backed view about a text, which is a different idea at a different depth.

draft.title: Supporting a view in discussion
card: A view is your judgement about a text, such as what it suggests or how well it works. State it clearly so others know your position.
Back the view with an example from the text. Name the moment, character or technique, and say how it supports your view.
Respond to what others have said. You can agree and build on a point, or disagree politely and give your reason.
A strong contribution joins all three: a view, an example and a link to another speaker. A view with no example is only an opinion, and a speech that ignores the others is not a discussion.
draft.remember: Say your view, prove it with an example, and answer the others.

a.q: Which contribution to a class discussion of a novel is the strongest?
opts: The narrator seems unreliable: she contradicts herself in chapter two. Sam, that makes her hard to trust
The narrator is unreliable. I have always felt that way, and nothing will change my mind
I liked this novel a lot, and the narrator was one of the best parts for me
Sam and Priya both think the narrator is honest, so the rest of us should agree
a.why: It states a view, backs it with an example from the text and responds to Sam. The second option has a view but no example and ignores others. The third gives only a feeling, with no example or link.
a.clue: Look for a view, an example and a reply to someone.

b.q: In a discussion of a poem, Jo says the poem shows loneliness. Mina wants to disagree and still make a strong contribution. What should she say?
opts: I see hope, Jo: the final line mentions a sunrise, which outweighs the lonely images
I disagree with Jo. The poem is really about hope, so loneliness is the wrong reading
Jo, you are wrong about this poem, and most others here probably agree with me
I see hope, Jo, though I have not looked closely at the poem and cannot say why
b.why: Mina responds to Jo, states her own view and backs it with an example from the poem. The second option disagrees and gives a view but no example. Disagreement is allowed, but it needs a reason from the text.
b.clue: Disagreeing is fine, but it still needs evidence.

a.q: In a class discussion of a novel, Sam says the narrator seems honest. Which reply is the strongest contribution?
opts: Sam, I doubt her: she lies to her sister in chapter two
I think the ending is weak, as chapter ten rushes the twist
Sam, I doubt she is honest, but I cannot point to a moment
Sam, I agree with you, as most people in the class do
a.why: The reply about the narrator lying to her sister answers Sam's point, states a view and backs it with an example from the text. The reply about the rushed ending has a view and an example, but it ignores what Sam said, so it is not a response.
a.clue: Look for a view, an example and a reply to Sam's point.

b.q: In a discussion of a poem, Jo says the poem shows loneliness. Mina wants to disagree and still make a strong contribution. What should she say?
opts: Jo, I see hope: the poem ends on a sunrise, a new start
Jo, I see hope, and the poem has four stanzas of six lines
Jo, I see hope, because that is just how it felt to me
Jo, you are wrong, and the rest of the class agrees with me
b.why: The sunrise reply responds to Jo, states a view and gives an example that shows why the poem suggests hope. The reply about four stanzas names a detail, but the detail does not support the view, so it is not real evidence.
b.clue: An example only counts if it shows why the view is right.
